42862255.label: Objectives
42862255.text: To investigate the correlation between tissue stiffness, as measured across various target tissues using multifrequency three-dimensional magnetic resonance elastography (3D-MRE), and tumor responses to transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), as well as post-treatment prognosis in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

42862255.label: Methods
42862255.text: HCC patients scheduled for TACE treatment were prospectively recruited and received multifrequency 3D-MRE before the initiation of TACE procedure. Measurements of tumor stiffness (TS), liver stiffness (LS), and spleen stiffness (SS) were conducted at frequencies of 60 Hz and 30 Hz, respectively. Treatment response was assessed using the mRECIST. Patient follow-up was conducted to evaluate overall survival outcomes.

42862255.label: Results
42862255.text: The final patient cohort consisted of 43 patients (mean age: 56.66±10.13 years; 34 males), including 16 non-responders and 27 responders. Non-responders exhibited significantly elevated TS (4.10±2.54 vs. 2.68±1.61kPa, p=0.035), LS (2.88±1.43 vs. 1.97±0.59kPa, p=0.026), and SS (4.03±0.90 vs. 3.13±1.08kPa, p=0.008) at the frequency of 30Hz. Firth's penalized univariable logistic analysis identified age (adjusted odds ratio [OR]=0.93, P=0.036), tumor number (OR=0.69, P=0.035), LS at 60Hz (OR=0.79, p=0.046), TS at 30Hz (OR=0.73, p=0.037), LS at 30Hz (OR=0.44, p=0.008), and SS at 30Hz (OR=0.44, P=0.009) as potential predictors of treatment response. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for predicting treatment response was 0.69 for age, tumor number and TS at 30Hz, 0.67 for LS at both 60Hz and 30Hz, and 0.75 for SS at 30Hz. Univariable Cox regression identified TS at both 60Hz (hazard ratio=1.15, p=0.014) and 30Hz (hazard ratio=1.40, p=0.010) as potential predictors of overall survival.

42862255.label: Conclusion
42862255.text: Spleen stiffness measured at 30 Hz via 3D-MRE may serve as a potential predictor of treatment response to TACE in HCC patients, whereas tumor stiffness measured at both 60Hz and 30Hz appears to correlate with overall survival. Further research is necessary to validate these preliminary associations.

42891705.label: Objectives
42891705.text: To reassess pretreatment photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT)-derived normalized iodine concentration (NIC) in an expanded rectal-cancer cohort, using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) as a within-cohort reference marker for histopathologic treatment response.

42891705.label: Methods
42891705.text: This single-center retrospective study included 63 patients with rectal adenocarcinoma who underwent pretreatment pelvic MRI and contrast-enhanced PCCT, followed by neoadjuvant treatment and surgical resection. Dworak tumor regression grades 0-1 were classified as poor response (n = 22) and grades 2-4 as moderate/good response (n = 41). MRI and PCCT were performed a median of 3 days apart (IQR, 1-4.5). The previously reported NIC threshold of ≥ 0.36 was reassessed without re-optimization. Twenty-one of 63 patients overlapped with the preceding pilot cohort; therefore, the present study is an expanded reassessment rather than an independent external validation.

42891705.label: Results
42891705.text: Twenty-two patients showed poor response and 41 moderate/good response. ADC interobserver agreement was excellent (ICC, 0.959; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90-0.98). In the 61 patients with paired numeric NIC measurements from both observers, NIC interobserver agreement was also excellent (ICC, 0.905; bootstrap 95% CI, 0.858-0.936). Mean ADC was lower in poor responders than in moderate/good responders (0.876 ± 0.186 vs. 1.035 ± 0.208 × 10⁻³ mm²/s; p = 0.003; AUC, 0.738; 95% CI, 0.608-0.867). NIC did not differ between groups (median, 0.313 vs. 0.370; p = 0.91; AUC, 0.509; 95% CI, 0.362-0.656). Applying the previously published NIC threshold ≥ 0.36 yielded sensitivity 53.7%, specificity 63.6%, and accuracy 57.1% for Dworak grades 2-4. Adding NIC to ADC did not improve model fit (likelihood-ratio p = 0.601).

42891705.label: Conclusion
42891705.text: In this exploratory expanded cohort, lower pretreatment ADC was associated with Dworak grades 0-1. Single-phase portal-venous NIC measured with the described two-dimensional ROI approach did not reproduce the high performance reported in the pilot study and showed no evidence of improved model fit beyond ADC in this cohort. These findings require independent prospective validation.

42925455.label: Objective
42925455.text: Multi-pinhole SPECT offers improved sensitivity and spatial resolution; however, overlapping projection data and multiple sources of physical image degradation remain major challenges. We propose a novel convolutional neural network (CNN)-based framework that simultaneously separates overlapping projections and corrects for gamma-ray attenuation, scatter, quantum noise, and aperture effects without requiring an attenuation coefficient map (μ-map) derived from X-ray CT.

42925455.label: Methods
42925455.text: Brain imaging was investigated using a three-detector stationary SPECT system equipped with a 44-pinhole collimator (pinhole diameter, 2 mm). A U-Net++-based CNN was trained to separate overlapping projections and correct multiple physical degradation factors. The input comprised overlapping projection data generated by Monte Carlo photon transport simulations, whereas the target data were ideal projections calculated using a ray-tracing method without projection overlap, attenuation, scatter, or other physical effects. A publicly available brain image dataset comprising 60 cases was used for training (4,050 images), validating (144 images) and testing (126 images). Corrected projections were reconstructed using the maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization (ML-EM) method. Image quality was evaluated visually and quantitatively using the normalized mean squared error (NMSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), and regional uptake bias. One-sided t-tests were performed against images reconstructed with 11 non-overlapping pinholes, and a fan-beam collimator method.

42925455.label: Results
42925455.text: The proposed framework accurately separated overlapping projections and simultaneously suppressed attenuation, scatter, quantum noise, and aperture-related degradation. It also reduced artifacts caused by the limited number of projections. The proposed method with a quasi-stationary data acquisition achieved an NMSE of 0.18 ± 0.02, a PSNR of 18.42 ± 0.69 dB, and an SSIM of 0.81 ± 0.04, outperforming 11-pinhole reconstruction (NMSE, 0.23 ± 0.05; PSNR, 15.72 ± 1.27 dB; SSIM, 0.78 ± 0.06) and fan-beam reconstruction with a 20-fold longer acquisition time (NMSE, 0.20 ± 0.03; PSNR, 15.93 ± 1.12 dB; SSIM, 0.78 ± 0.05).

42925455.label: Conclusions
42925455.text: The proposed CNN-based framework enables simultaneous projection separation and correction of multiple physical degradation factors in stationary multi-pinhole SPECT without CT-derived attenuation correction. This approach may reduce radiation exposure and system cost while enabling high-sensitivity, high-resolution, and quantitatively accurate SPECT imaging.

42957205.text: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has shown remarkable efficacy in advanced metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. However, salivary gland toxicity is a major dose-limiting adverse effect, particularly with α-emitting radionuclides such as 225Ac. Although tandem therapy with combined [225Ac]Ac- and [177Lu]Lu-labeled PSMA-targeted RPT in a single low-activity cycle may address certain challenges, effective salivary gland protection remains crucial. In this study, we explored the use of botulinum toxin (BTX) type A (incobotulinumtoxinA) plus transdermal scopolamine as a protective strategy to mitigate salivary gland uptake of PSMA radioligands. Methods: IncobotulinumtoxinA was injected percutaneously, with increasing dosages of up to 300 units distributed into the parotid and submandibular glands under ultrasound guidance, a mean of 24 d before scheduled tandem PSMA RPT. Transdermal scopolamine was applied from 72 h before RPT until 2 h after RPT. Molecular imaging was conducted as per PSMA RPT protocol, with pretreatment PSMA PET/CT to confirm ligand uptake and follow-up PET/CT for restaging. SPECT/CT was conducted as imaging after RPT. PET SUVmean or SPECT counts were measured, and ratios of injected-to-noninjected contralateral glands were calculated and compared before and after BTX. Results: Fourteen patients (mean age, 68.0 ± 8.1 y) were included; 1 patient received 2 injections before his treatment, and another underwent 2 tandem RPT cycles, with BTX administered before each cycle. Mean cumulative administered activity was 5.05 ± 1.09 GBq for 177Lu and 6.87 ± 3.14 MBq for 225Ac. Combination therapy with incobotulinumtoxinA plus transdermal scopolamine was associated with lower PSMA radioligand uptake in BTX-treated salivary glands relative to untreated contralateral glands, with mean reductions of approximately 30% in parotid glands and 17% in submandibular glands compared with untreated glands. Up to 300 units of incobotulinumtoxinA distributed among the major salivary glands was safe. No patient discontinued tandem PSMA therapy because of xerostomia, and no grade 3 or 4 toxicities were observed during PSMA RPT. Conclusion: BTX plus transdermal scopolamine is a promising strategy to reduce salivary gland uptake during PSMA RPT. This approach enhances patient quality of life after PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy, particularly with α-emitting radionuclides, while preserving its excellent therapeutic efficacy.

42975305.text: Background The incidence of lymph node (LN) metastasis in patients with part-solid nodules (PSNs) is known to be low, which makes the intraoperative evaluation of LNs a controversial issue. Purpose To investigate the incidence of LN metastasis and explore clinical-radiologic predicting factors for LN metastasis in PSN lung adenocarcinomas with a solid portion diameter of 30.0 mm or less in a large surgical study sample. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included patients with part-solid lung adenocarcinomas with solid portion diameters of 30.0 mm or less on preoperative CT images from July 2023 to December 2024. For each PSN, overall tumor size, solid portion diameter, consolidation-to-tumor ratio (CTR), location, margin, shape, spiculation, lobulation, pleural retraction, bubble-like lucency, and air bronchogram were independently evaluated by two chest radiologists blinded to clinical information and pathology results. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Results This study included 1444 patients (median age, 59 years; IQR, 51-67 years; 931 women). The frequency of LN metastasis was 4.7% (68 of 1444 patients). None of the 115 patients with a CTR of 0.25 or less had LN metastasis (N1: 0 of 115; N2: 0 of 115). Rarely (0.2%, one of 552), LN metastasis was found in patients with a solid portion diameter of 6.0 mm or less. Solid portion diameter was the only independent predictor of LN metastasis (odds ratio, 1.25; 95% CI: 1.20, 1.31) in multivariable analysis and showed a superior diagnostic performance compared with CTR (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.86 [95% CI: 0.82, 0.90] vs 0.75 [95% CI: 0.68, 0.80]; P < .001), along with better calibration (Brier score, 0.039 vs 0.044) and greater net benefit. The clinical actionable cutoff for solid portion diameter was 7.3 mm (sensitivity, 95.6%; specificity, 49.6%). Conclusion Solid portion diameter had a superior diagnostic performance compared with CTR in predicting LN metastasis in patients with part-solid lung adenocarcinomas of solid portion diameter of 30.0 mm or less at CT.

42989855.label: Background
42989855.text: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) may induce redistribution of the fetal circulation to preserve perfusion of vital organs. Reduced hepatic delivery of oxygen- and nutrient-rich blood may cause volumetric and morphological remodeling.

42989855.label: Purpose
42989855.text: To quantify fetal liver volume and morphology in FGR and assess associations with adverse neonatal outcomes.

42989855.label: Population
42989855.text: Ninety-two singleton pregnancies: 36 FGR cases (prospective) and 56 appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) controls (retrospective).

42989855.label: Field strength/sequence
42989855.text: 3-T, True Fast Imaging with Steady-State Free Precession (TrueFISP) for fetal liver and body imaging, and TrueFISP or Half-Fourier Acquisition Single-shot Turbo Spin-Echo for brain imaging.

42989855.label: Assessment
42989855.text: The fetal liver, body, and brain were segmented using deep learning tools. Liver volume, liver-to-body and brain-to-liver volume ratios, and 12 liver PyRadiomics shape features were assessed. Neonates were followed for composite adverse neonatal outcomes (CANO) until discharge.

42989855.label: Statistical tests
42989855.text: Linear regression assessed associations with gestational age in AGA fetuses. Linear mixed-effects models compared groups, adjusting for gestational age and fetal sex. Univariable logistic regression assessed associations with CANO. Benjamini-Hochberg correction controlled the false discovery rate at 0.05.

42989855.label: Results
42989855.text: FGR fetuses had significantly lower liver volume than AGA fetuses (74.95 ± 1.76 vs. 114.89 ± 2.18 cm3), lower liver-to-body ratio (0.053 ± 0.001 vs. 0.057 ± 0.001), and higher brain-to-liver ratio (2.637 ± 0.085 vs. 1.978 ± 0.047). FGR fetuses demonstrated significantly less elongated liver geometry, (10.7% higher PyRadiomics elongation values) and had a significantly higher surface-to-volume ratio (11.9%). CANO occurred in 30/92 neonates (27 FGR, 3 AGA). Higher brain-to-liver ratio (OR = 4.12, 95% CI: 1.93-8.77), PyRadiomics elongation values (less elongated geometry; OR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.26-3.30), PyRadiomics flatness values (less flattened geometry; OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.07-2.65), and surface-to-volume ratio (OR = 3.26, 95% CI: 1.80-5.90) were significantly associated with CANO.

42989855.label: Data conclusion
42989855.text: FGR was associated with reduced fetal liver size and altered geometry, which were associated with neonatal morbidity.

42993105.label: Background
42993105.text: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) enables assessment of aortic valve tissue composition, providing insights into disease progression and helping predict outcomes in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis (AS). The authors aimed to develop a deep learning system for CTA-based quantification of aortic fibrotic and calcific tissue, validate its agreement with expert manual analysis and histopathology, and evaluate its value for outcome prediction.

42993105.label: Methods
42993105.text: This international, multicenter study included 1,674 patients who underwent CTA at 9 sites. A deep learning model based on the nnU-Net architecture was trained in 468 patients and applied to an external test set of 1,206 patients, including 29 with valve histology and 12 with serial CTA. In 1,165 patients with clinical outcomes, prognostic value was assessed adjusting for clinical, echocardiographic, and procedural covariates.

42993105.label: Results
42993105.text: Deep learning-enabled tissue composition analysis was rapid (1.35 ± 0.4 min vs 7.2 ± 1.2 min for experts) with excellent agreement vs expert assessment (r = 0.915; intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC] = 0.913), histology (r = 0.909; ICC = 0.905), and scan-rescan reproducibility (r = 0.999; ICC = 0.999). In the external cohort, 469 patients (40%) died over 4.1 ± 1.1 years of follow-up. Fibrotic tissue volume (adjusted HR [aHR] 1.42 per IQR increase; P < 0.001), calcific tissue attenuation (aHR 1.02 per 25 HU increase; P = 0.005), left ventricular ejection fraction (aHR 1.10 per 5% decrease; P < 0.001), life-threatening bleeding (aHR: 1.96; P = 0.003), major vascular complication (aHR: 1.51; P = 0.042) and postprocedural peak pressure gradient (aHR 1.03 per 1 mm Hg increase; P < 0.001) independently predicted mortality. Patients in the highest tertile of fibrotic tissue volume (>0.940 cm3) had a 2-fold higher risk of death (aHR: 2.0; P < 0.001), whereas patients with dense calcific tissue attenuation (>885 HU) had a 1.5-fold higher risk of death.

42993105.label: Conclusions
42993105.text: Deep learning enables rapid quantification of aortic valve fibrotic and calcific tissue from CTA, demonstrating excellent agreement with both expert CTA and histological assessments. Quantitative analysis of aortic tissue composition provides additional prognostic value for all-cause mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement in multicenter external evaluation.

43003605.label: Background
43003605.text: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) calcification affects clinical outcomes by causing transcatheter heart valve (THV) deformation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, a computed tomography (CT)-based scoring system for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation has not been established.

43003605.label: Objectives
43003605.text: This study sought to develop a cardiac CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation.

43003605.label: Methods
43003605.text: This single-center retrospective study included consecutive patients with BAV who underwent TAVR using contemporary balloon-expandable valves between January 2016 and December 2024 and who had preprocedural and postprocedural CT imaging. The BAV TAVR-risk score integrated calcification severity and distribution across valve leaflets, raphe, annulus, and left ventricular outflow tract, quantified using a fixed HU-850 threshold of detection on contrast-enhanced CT scans. Score thresholds were derived by receiver operating curve analysis with Youden index optimization. Patients were categorized into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk score groups.

43003605.label: Results
43003605.text: Among 321 patients (median follow-up: 1,825 days; Q1-Q3: 765-1,825 days), 56 (17.4%) were classified into the high-risk score group. Both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV occurred in 49 of the 321 patients (15.3%) and were predominantly observed in the high-risk score group. However, in the low-risk score group, 149 of 155 patients (96.1%) demonstrated no underexpansion or eccentricity of the THV. A high BAV TAVR-risk score independently predicted both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV (OR: 89.13; 95% CI: 35.02-226.83; P < 0.001).

43003605.label: Conclusions
43003605.text: This CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score provides a systematic method to precisely quantify BAV severity which reliably predicts THV deformation for BAV patients with contemporary balloon-expandable valves and may help guide decision-making in this challenging population.

43018705.label: Purpose
43018705.text: To develop and externally validate a peri-ablational contrast-enhanced CT radiomics model for predicting early hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression after microwave ablation (MWA) and to assess its incremental value over clinical predictors.

43018705.label: Methods
43018705.text: This retrospective multicenter study included 376 patients in training (n = 235), internal validation (n = 60), and external validation (n = 81) cohorts. Early progression was defined as local tumor progression or new intrahepatic HCC within 1 year after MWA. Radiomics features were extracted from 5-mm peri-ablational regions on multiphasic CT obtained 1-2 months after MWA. Six machine-learning algorithms and phase combinations were evaluated. The selected radiomics model was combined with independent clinical predictors. Discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and model interpretability were assessed.

43018705.label: Results
43018705.text: The arterial-plus-portal venous phase (AP + PP) multilayer perceptron model achieved AUCs of 0.857, 0.815, and 0.903 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively, with performance comparable to the three-phase model. Log10 AFP and tumor size > 2 cm were independent clinical predictors. The combined clinical-radiomics model achieved AUCs of 0.926, 0.884, and 0.963, respectively. In external validation, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 84.2%, 96.8%, and 93.8%, respectively. SHAP analysis identified the radiomics score as the most influential predictor.

43018705.label: Conclusion
43018705.text: Peri-ablational AP + PP CT radiomics combined with AFP and tumor size demonstrated good discrimination for early HCC progression after MWA and may facilitate individualized risk assessment, pending further validation.

43034255.text: Acute aortic syndromes (AAS) are a group of aortic pathologies with high morbidity and mortality. In the emergency setting, an accurate diagnosis is usually achieved by aortic computed tomography angiography (CTA). Recently, reporting and management guidelines have evolved due to modifications in surgical techniques and the expansion in utilization of endovascular techniques. This being said, radiologists require a more in-depth knowledge of key points to report to surgeons, their clinical implications, and some insights into available imaging-guided treatment options. Given the urgent nature of AAS, the need for rapid, detailed, and standardized reporting is crucial. In this review, we aim to introduce a step-by-step approach to accurate reporting of AAS, discussing recent guidelines and the role of imaging in the preprocedural evaluation of each disease entity (namely, intramural hematoma, penetrating aortic ulcer, and aortic dissection). Additionally, we will highlight the role of key imaging findings in the management of each disease entity. KEY POINTS: Question Acute aortic syndromes require rapid, sufficiently detailed, and accurate diagnosis to allow for timely patient management. Findings In this article, we propose a step-by-step approach using a structured reporting checklist. Clinical relevance Using a stepwise approach will allow timely reporting, give important details, and help guide further patient care.

43050605.label: Background
43050605.text: The routine clinical implementation of patient-specific dosimetry in 177Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy can be challenging due to the need for multiple-time-point posttherapy SPECT/CT imaging to estimate time-integrated activity (TIA). Single-time-point (STP) approaches offer a more practical alternative, although their accuracy has yet to be fully established. This study aimed to evaluate existing analytical STP methods and to assess the feasibility and performance of a machine learning (ML) framework.

43050605.label: Patients and methods
43050605.text: Thirty-four patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer undergoing 177Lu-PSMA-617 therapy were retrospectively analyzed. Reference TIAs were derived from multiple-time-point 177Lu SPECT/CT imaging at 3 or 4 time points (TPs) postinjection (TP1: 0.7-2.1 h, TP2: day 1-2, TP3: day 3-4, TP4: day 5-7) in cycle 1 for 147 tumors, 64 kidneys, and 65 parotid glands using monoexponential or biexponential fitting. Analytical STP methods, proposed by Hänscheid and Madsen, were evaluated across different TPs. For each organ, a ML model was developed using a residual learning approach, in which the log-transformed ratio between reference TIAs and analytical STP TIA estimates was modeled. Input features included combinations of STP SPECT-derived parameters, baseline 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET-derived biomarkers (for individual structures and whole-body tumor volume), and clinical variables. Model performance was evaluated by using multiple quantitative metrics within a 10-times repeated 5-fold nested cross-validation framework and compared with purely analytic STP approaches. Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations.

43050605.label: Results
43050605.text: Analytical methods showed strong performance at optimal imaging TPs (TP2 for kidney/parotid, and TP3 for tumor), with the largest errors observed at early imaging (TP1). Overall, ML models provided modest improvement over analytical methods across structures at most TPs. The best performance was achieved using a ML model combining PET/SPECT imaging features with analytical TIA estimates. The mean percentage errors of the models, across TPs, ranged from -1.7 ± 17.9% (TP2) to 7.4 ± 65.3% (TP1) for kidneys, -0.4 ± 12.1% (TP2) to 4.5 ± 26.7% (TP4) for parotid glands, and 1.4 ± 14.8% (TP3) to -4.1 ± 100.5% (TP1) for tumors. Within the present cohort and modeling framework, the inclusion of clinical variables did not significantly improve model performance. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis showed that the ML models applied a positive correction to the analytical TIA estimates at early imaging TPs and a negative correction at late TPs.

43050605.label: Conclusions
43050605.text: Analytical STP methods yield accurate TIA estimates when applied at appropriate imaging TPs. ML models that integrate analytical estimates with imaging features provide modest improvements in accuracy with less sensitivity to TP selection. However, optimal timing remained structure-dependent, requiring a compromise when a single acquisition is used. These findings support the potential of ML-driven STP dosimetry in 177Lu-PSMA-617 radiopharmaceutical therapy to enable more flexible and clinically feasible workflows, pending further validation with larger and more diverse data sets.

43077105.label: Purpose
43077105.text: To evaluate the feasibility and additional value of total-body PET image-derived pharmacokinetics over venous blood-sampling method in investigating non-tumor tissue and lesion kinetics of the PD-L1-targeted tracer [68​Ga]Ga-NOTA-SNA002 in patients with malignant tumors.

43077105.label: Methods
43077105.text: Patients with solid tumors underwent a 60-min dynamic total-body PET acquisition following [68​Ga]Ga-NOTA-SNA002 injection, and a 20-min static scan at 120 min post-injection, accompanied by serial venous blood sampling. Systemic PK parameters were estimated via noncompartmental analysis based on time-concentration curves from venous blood sampling and image-derived venous vascular regions using a single-sample calibration, and the PK parameters obtained from the two methods were compared. To characterize kinetic parameters, time-activity curves (TACs) of non-tumor tissues and lung lesions were fitted using compartment models. Lesions' kinetic metrics and standardized uptake value (SUV) were compared after stratification by tumor proportion score (TPS; < 50% vs. ≥ 50%).

43077105.label: Results
43077105.text: Image-derived maximum concentration (Cmax) was significantly higher and time to Cmax (Tmax) was significantly shorter than those obtained from venous blood sampling. No significant between-method differences were observed for the remaining PK parameters, except SVC-derived clearance (CL; 2.35 ± 0.69 vs. 2.69 ± 0.90 L/h, P = 0.016). The relative differences were within 18% for right atrium (RA) and within 19% for superior vena cava (SVC) for these parameters. Lesions with high TPS (≥ 50%) demonstrated significantly elevated K1 (0.51 ± 0.17 vs. 0.11 ± 0.09 mL/cm3/min, P = 0.009) and k2 (6.06 ± 1.76 vs. 2.19 ± 1.60 min-1, P = 0.009) compared to those with low TPS (< 50%). Additionally, dynamic [68​Ga]Ga-NOTA-SNA002 PET provided information on tracer retention in non-tumor tissues and lesions.

43077105.label: Conclusion
43077105.text: Total-body dynamic PET imaging with a single-sample calibration provides PK data comparable to conventional venous blood sampling while simultaneously characterizing tissue kinetic profiles throughout the body. Additionally, these kinetic parameters may offer complementary value for the stratification of lesion-level PD-L1 expression and the preliminary assessment of immunotherapy response.

43077105.label: Clinical trial registration
43077105.text: This phase I clinical trial was approved by the National Medical Products Administration of China and was registered at www.chinadrugtrials.org.cn (registry number: CTR20232251).
